dialogues.narration_planned: Let's start at the very foundation. Imagine you have a random number generator. Every time you press a button, it gives you a number. dialogues.narration_planned: The most important distribution in all of deep learning is the Gaussian, also called the normal distribution. It's this bell curve, and it's defined by just two numbers. Mu, the mean — it's the center, the peak of the bell. Watch what happens when I slide mu to the right: the entire curve shifts. Mu controls where the distribution lives. Sigma, the standard deviation — it controls how spread out the distribution is. Large sigma means samples could land far from the center. Small sigma means they cluster tightly around the mean. Here's a fact you'll use constantly: sixty-eight percent of all samples fall within one sigma of the mean. Ninety-five percent within two sigma. This is written as N of x given mu and sigma squared. Aswin, remember this formula — in your video generation model, the latent space will be a Gaussian. Every single frame your model generates starts as a sample from this distribution.

dialogues.narration_planned: Now here's where most people get confused, so pay close attention. The y-axis of this curve is called probability density, not probability. This is critical. The height of the curve at any single point is NOT the probability of that point. In a continuous distribution, the probability of any exact value — like x equals exactly one point zero zero zero — is actually zero. Probability lives in areas, not heights. The probability that x falls between one point zero and one point one is this shaded area — the integral of the density function over that interval. And the total area under the entire curve always equals exactly one. Why does this matter for your video model? Because when we talk about sampling from a distribution, we're asking: in which region of this curve does our random number land? The density tells us where samples are concentrated. High density means samples cluster there. Low density means they avoid it.

dialogues.narration_planned: Now let's talk about conditional probability — probability with context. Here's the idea. Suppose we're generating video frames. Forty percent of all possible frames contain a face — that's P of A. Thirty percent are well-lit — that's P of B. And twenty percent have both — a face AND good lighting. Now here's the question: if I tell you a frame IS well-lit, what's the probability it contains a face? This is P of A given B — the conditional probability. Visually, when we learn B happened, our universe shrinks. We're no longer looking at all possible frames — only the well-lit ones. Within that smaller universe, what fraction has faces? It's twenty percent out of thirty percent, which gives us sixty-seven percent. The formula is P of A given B equals P of A intersection B divided by P of B. This concept is the heartbeat of generative models, because generation is all about conditioning: generate a frame GIVEN this text prompt, GIVEN the previous frame, GIVEN this style.
chunks: Look at the diagram on the screen, notice how it's a large square representing the full sample space, divided into colored regions, with region A in blue, region B in green, and the overlap of A and B in teal.

See where the teal overlap is circled with a formula, Aswin, this is where we calculate the probability of A given B, and it's essentially the probability of both A and B happening divided by the probability of just B.

Notice how the animation starts by highlighting region B and graying out the rest, which means we know that B has happened, and now we're looking at the probability of A happening within that highlighted region, it's like zooming in on a specific part of the sample space.

Now, what would happen if the teal overlap was really small compared to the entire green region, would that change our calculation of the probability of A given B, and why do you think that is, let's think about it for a moment.

dialogues.narration_planned: Bayes' theorem is just conditional probability with a power move. It lets you flip the direction of conditioning. Here it is. P of A given B equals P of B given A, times P of A, divided by P of B. Let me translate each piece. P of A is the prior — your belief before seeing any evidence. P of B given A is the likelihood — if A were true, how probable is the evidence you observed? P of B is the evidence term — how probable is what you saw, overall? And P of A given B is the posterior — your updated belief after seeing the evidence. Think of it as a learning machine. You start with a guess — the prior. You observe reality — the likelihood. You combine them, and out comes a better, data-informed belief — the posterior. Aswin, this exact framework is how your video generation model will reason. It starts with a prior over latent codes, observes training data, and updates to a posterior that captures the structure of real videos.
chunks: Look at the equation on the screen, notice how it's broken down into four parts, each with its own labeled box and analogy to help us understand what's going on. See where it says Prior, that's what we believed before seeing any evidence, and it's a crucial part of the equation.

Now, Aswin, let's think about what we just saw in the animation with the balance scale, where the Prior and the Likelihood are on either side, and how they tip the scale to give us the Posterior. This is kind of like weighing our options, and it's really cool to see it in action.

Notice how the equation is trying to find the probability of A given B, that's the Posterior, and it's doing it by multiplying the probability of B given A, which is the Likelihood, by the Prior, and then dividing by the overall probability of B, which is the Evidence. What would happen if the Evidence was really unlikely, would that change our Posterior?

Look at the way the terms are related to each other, it's like a little story, we start with what we know, the Prior, then we get some new information, the Likelihood, and we use that to update what we know, the Posterior, and it all hinges on the Evidence, so let's take a moment to think about how this all fits together, and how it connects to what we saw in the heatmap earlier.

dialogues.narration_planned: Here's where Bayes meets your video model directly. In a generative model, you have a latent code z — a compressed representation — and a video frame x. The decoder gives you P of x given z: given a latent code, generate a frame. That's the easy direction. But the hard question is the reverse: given a video frame, what latent code produced it? That's P of z given x — the posterior. Bayes' theorem says you can compute it, but there's a catch. You need P of x — the probability of the video frame across ALL possible latent codes. And that requires summing over an astronomically large space of z values. It's intractable. You literally cannot compute it. This is the fundamental problem that gave birth to variational autoencoders and diffusion models. They don't compute the true posterior — they approximate it. And the tool they use to measure how good that approximation is? That's K L divergence, which we're about to learn.

dialogues.narration_planned: K L divergence. This measures how different two distributions are, but with a twist — it's not symmetric. Here's the formula: D K L of P from Q equals the sum over all x of P of x times log of P of x over Q of x. Let me break it down visually. For each possible value x, you take the ratio of P of x to Q of x. Then you take the log. If P and Q agree, the log is zero — no penalty. If P is high but Q is low — meaning Q underestimates where P puts its mass — the log ratio is large and positive. That's a big penalty. Now the crucial part: you weight each penalty by P of x. This means K L divergence only cares about mismatches where P has significant mass. If P is near zero somewhere, it doesn't matter what Q does there. This asymmetry is fundamental. K L of P from Q is NOT the same as K L of Q from P. In your video model's training, this asymmetry determines whether the model covers all real videos or just generates a few really good ones.
chunks: Look at the equation on the screen, notice how it's the KL divergence formula, which is a measure of the difference between two probability distributions, and see where it says D KL P or Q equals the sum of P of x times the log of P of x divided by Q of x.

Now that we have the formula, let's take a look at the bar chart below, notice how each bar represents a value of x, and see the blue bars showing the probability distribution P of x, and the orange bars showing the probability distribution Q of x, Aswin.

Notice how for each x, the ratio of P of x to Q of x is computed, and shown as a green bar, and then the log of each ratio is taken, which gives us bars that are above zero where P is greater than Q, and below zero where P is less than Q - now, can you imagine what would happen if P and Q were the same, would we still see any bars above or below zero?

See where each log ratio bar is now weighted by P of x, so the tall P of x bars are amplifying the corresponding log ratio, and the shorter P of x bars are reducing it, which is essential in calculating the KL divergence, and this weighted sum is what gives us the final measure of the difference between the two distributions.

dialogues.narration_planned: Now watch K L divergence in action inside a variational autoencoder — the ancestor of every modern video generation model. The true posterior — the real answer to 'what latent code explains this video frame' — is this complicated, multi-peaked distribution on the left. We can't compute it exactly. So we train a neural network — the encoder — to produce an approximate posterior Q, which is a simple Gaussian. K L divergence measures the gap between Q and the true posterior. During training, we minimize this gap. Watch Q evolve: its mean shifts, its spread adjusts, step by step getting closer to the true distribution. The V A E loss function has two terms: reconstruction loss, which says 'generate frames that look real,' and K L divergence from Q to the prior, which says 'keep the latent space organized as a nice Gaussian.' That K L term is why you can sample from a Gaussian at generation time and get coherent outputs. Without it, the latent space would be chaotic, and random samples would produce garbage.

dialogues.narration_planned: Next concept: expectation. This is the probability-weighted average of a quantity, and you'll use it everywhere in deep learning. Here's the intuition. Take a distribution and pick several x values. Each has a probability weight — how likely it is to be sampled. The expectation E of x is the weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, sum them up. Visually, it's the center of mass. If you cut out the distribution curve from cardboard and balanced it on your finger, the balance point is the expectation. But here's the powerful part: you can take the expectation of ANY function of x, not just x itself. E of x squared? Weight each x squared by its probability. E of some neural network output given x? Same idea — weight by probability. In generative models, the training objective is almost always written as an expectation: 'the expected reconstruction error' or 'the expected log likelihood.' Understanding this concept unlocks every loss function you'll ever see.
chunks: Look at the animation on the screen, notice how each x value is lifting off the axis and scaling in size according to its probability weight, it's really cool to see the weighted average come together like this. See where all these scaled values are merging into a single point on the number line, that's the expectation, a key concept we've been discussing.

Now, Aswin, take a glance at the physical analogy below the animation, it's a seesaw or balance beam with weights placed at various positions, this is a great way to think about the expectation, as if we're finding the balance point of all these weights. Look at how this animation connects to what we saw earlier with the directed graphical model, we're still exploring the idea of probabilities and how they influence the outcome, but now we're seeing it in a more dynamic way, with the weighted average being calculated right before our eyes, it's really powerful stuff.

dialogues.narration_planned: Here's the problem. In theory, computing an expectation requires an integral over the entire distribution. For high-dimensional distributions — like the distribution of video frames — this integral is impossibly hard. Enter Monte Carlo estimation. The idea is brilliantly simple. Instead of computing the integral exactly, just draw random samples from the distribution, evaluate your function at each sample, and average the results. That average converges to the true expectation. Watch: with five samples, our estimate is rough — big error bars. With fifty, it's getting there. With five hundred, we're close. The convergence rate is one over root N — to halve your error, you need four times as many samples. Aswin, this is not just theory. Every time you train a neural network with stochastic gradient descent, you're doing Monte Carlo estimation. Your mini-batch of training examples? That's a Monte Carlo estimate of the true gradient. Every step of training your video model will rely on this principle.
chunks: Look at the animation on the screen, notice how the complex wavy function is overlaid on a distribution, and see where the sample points are drawn from, Aswin.

Notice how the exact integration is shown as an impossible shimmering integral sign, which tells us that computing the area under the curve is really tough for complex distributions, and that's where the Monte Carlo approximation comes in.

See where the sample points are drawn from the distribution and how the function is evaluated at each of those points, and then the average of those values is used to approximate the expected value, isn't it interesting to think about how this process can be repeated with more and more sample points to get a better approximation?

Now that we've seen how the Monte Carlo approximation works, look at the equation on the right side of the screen, notice how it's a simple sum of the function values at each sample point, divided by the number of sample points, which is a much more manageable calculation than trying to compute the exact integral.

dialogues.narration_planned: Time to code, Aswin. Let's make these concepts concrete with Python. First block: sampling from a Gaussian. This is the same K L divergence that appears in your V A E loss function.
